title: The breaking of the vessels
hook: the vessels couldn't hold the light and shattered, scattering sparks

segments.voice: Yesterday, tzimtzum: in Luria's teaching, the Infinite drew in to leave room for a world. Your line was make room. Where did you leave a little space for someone? Day one thousand one hundred eighty-four.

Deep in Genesis there's a list that's easy to skim. "And these are the kings that reigned in the land of Edom, before there reigned any king over the children of Israel." Then name after name. And after every name but the last, the same short note: he died, and another reigned in his stead. Kabbalists slowed down at that list. Kings who rose and fell before anything could last. To them it sounded like a hint of something at the very beginning: a first world that couldn't hold. Today's word.
screen: `A LIST OF KINGS.` → `HE REIGNED, AND HE DIED.` → `A WORLD THAT COULDN'T HOLD.`

segments.voice: Shevirat hakelim. The breaking of the vessels. It's the next scene in Luria's story, as Chaim Vital sets it down. Turn it four ways. First, the vessels. After the line of light entered the open space, it needed containers: vessels to hold it and give it shape. Second, the breaking. The light was too strong. Some of the vessels could not hold it, and they shattered. Their pieces fell, and with them fell sparks of the light, scattered downward. Kabbalists tied this to those kings of Edom: each one reigned, and each one died, a world that came and couldn't stay. Third, what's surprising. In this picture, the breaking happens before there are any people at all. No one's mistake sets it off. It sits inside the story of the beginning itself. Fourth, the sparks. The light didn't vanish when the vessels broke. It's still there, down among the shards, mixed in with ordinary things. Everything else in Luria's teaching turns on that. Some readers hear in it a word for a life: a marriage that came apart, a body that doesn't work the way it did, a plan that cracked down the middle. In Luria's picture, broken pieces aren't empty. They're where the light landed. Tomorrow, what the tradition says to do about that. Today, it's enough to know the shards are carrying something.
screen: `VESSELS TO HOLD THE LIGHT.` · `TOO STRONG: THEY SHATTERED.` · `BEFORE THERE WERE ANY PEOPLE.` · `SPARKS AMONG THE SHARDS.` · then, large: `BROKEN THINGS HOLD LIGHT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: accept one broken thing. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind something in your life that's cracked. Keep it small for today: a chipped mug, a friendship that cooled, a habit you keep dropping, a part of your body that aches. Don't try to fix it yet. Just let it be what it is: broken. Then, gently, look for any light still in it. A memory. Something it taught you. Someone it brought closer. If you find nothing, that's all right. Simply rest beside it, without turning away. The bell holds the time.
Shevirat hakelim. The breaking of the vessels: in Luria's story, vessels that couldn't hold the light shattered, and sparks fell with the pieces. Today's word.
Your line: broken things hold light. Today, when something cracks or goes wrong, before you sweep it up, look at it once more for what it's still carrying. Day one thousand one hundred eighty-four.

howItsDone: The breaking of the vessels is studied in Lurianic Kabbalah through Chaim Vital's writings, and Jewish teachers often bring it up when speaking about loss and brokenness.

myth: in Luria's story, the vessels break because people did wrong
the breaking comes before there are any people at all.
when the vessels broke, sparks of light fell with the pieces
the light was scattered, not lost.
in this teaching, the shards are empty
they hold the fallen sparks: everything else turns on that.

fork.setup: you are a vessel, made to hold the light. it pours in, stronger than you can hold. what does Luria's story say happens?
options: the vessel stretches and holds it all.
the vessel shatters, and sparks fall with the pieces.
the light turns back and leaves.
fork.reveal: the vessels broke, and sparks of light fell with the shards, scattered below but not lost.

original.note: Hebrew: the breaking of the vessels.

trapdoor: what you thought: a story about broken pottery.
what it means: in Luria's teaching, vessels made to hold the divine light shattered, and sparks fell into the world.
what a scholar hears: Vital's account of the shattering, read with the kings of Edom in Genesis 36, each of whom reigned and died.
recall: the book of creation, or formation

notes: Editor pass: hook opener 'Near the end of Genesis' changed to 'Deep in Genesis' (chapter 36 of 50 is not near the end, and 'Near the end of' also opens day 1186).
Genesis 36:31 quoted from JPS 1917; please confirm wording. Genesis 36:32–39 paraphrased: each king's reign is followed by 'and he died', except the last, Hadar.

The link between the kings of Edom and the broken vessels is attributed to 'kabbalists' (it appears in the Zohar's Idra passages and in Lurianic writing); please confirm and supply exact references if wanted.
Etz Chaim paraphrased on the vessels shattering and sparks falling; please supply the precise Sha'ar reference.
'No one's mistake sets it off' reflects the Lurianic sequence (shattering before Adam); confirm this is fair, since some teachings frame the breaking as purposeful within the divine plan.
Life applications (marriage, body, plan) are framed as 'some readers hear', not as Luria's teaching.
